0001: What is PWM and Why Cars

What is PWM and Why Cars

Pulse Width Modulation (PWM) is the primary method for controlling power delivery in modern vehicles. This lesson introduces the fundamentals of PWM and why it replaced analog/resistive control in automotive systems.

PWM Fundamentals

PWM works by switching a power source on and off very rapidly, varying the "width" of the "on" pulse to control the average power delivered to a load. This technique is essential for:

  • Controlling fan speed (radiator fans, blower motors)
  • Regulating fuel pump flow
  • Managing actuator power in ECU-controlled systems

PWM vs. Analog/Resistive Control

Historically, automotive engineering used analog resistive control for simple on/off functions. The shift to PWM offers significant advantages:

  • Higher efficiency - less power wasted as heat
  • Faster response times - digital switching is quicker
  • Better precision - duty cycle can be finely adjusted
  • Diagnosability - PWM signals can be measured and analyzed

Diagnosing PWM Signals

Using a multimeter or oscilloscope, technicians can measure:

  • Duty cycle - percentage of time the signal is high
  • Frequency - how many cycles per second
  • Voltage levels - high and low state voltages

These measurements help identify issues with PWM-controlled components like radiator fans, fuel pumps, and blower motors.
